paras: The lynching of Jesse Waldrop was the killing in early July 1881 of a 23-year-old man accused of raping and murdering a young bride, Mrs. Mitchell, by armed men who took him from a Georgia jail to the roadside spot where her body had been found. Early wire reports said he was hanged there, but a LaGrange correspondent and a Cincinnati Enquirer special said he was burned alive at a stake. Papers across the country told the story as deserved retribution, and two described Waldrop as white.

Most reports placed the murder in Randolph County, Alabama, where the woman, about nineteen and married a few months, was found on the road near her home with her throat cut. The Enquirer named her Carrie Knight, wife of Dr. John Mitchell, and dated the discovery June 29; other papers gave June 20. A LaGrange correspondent of the Columbus Times, quoted by the Savannah Morning News, instead described an outrage on "a most respectable white lady" west of Franklin, Heard County, Georgia, by "a white man" named Waldroup. Bite marks showing a missing front tooth turned suspicion on Waldrop, who had such a gap and had been seen nearby, and bloodhounds tracked him into Georgia.

Accounts of the capture differ, naming Franklin County, Hogansville, a house near Newnan, and, in the Courier-Journal special, "near Hopkinsville, in this State." He was jailed at Franklin, Georgia, and confessed the killing, though several reports said he denied the rape.

Most accounts dated the seizure Monday night, July 4, and put the party at about one hundred armed men; the Enquirer counted fifty, "not disguised," and the LaGrange correspondent about sixty. The jailer gave up the prisoner, in the Tribune's account because he feared refusal would cost him his life. According to the Enquirer, relatives of the dead woman guarded him on the way, and at the spot where the body had lain he was wired to a stake, surrounded with oil-soaked pine, and burned at midnight by one of those relatives as the men looked on. The Savannah Morning News, citing Columbus papers, said six hundred people attended.
In the hanging versions, the men set out to burn him but hanged him to the tree at whose foot the body was found.

Before he died, Waldrop accused a man named Mitchell, who was in the crowd and denied it, of offering him $75 to kill his own wife. A July 19 Atlanta dispatch named the man as Hal Mitchell and quoted Waldrop: "I killed Mrs. Mitchell by mistake, supposing she was the woman who swore against me." The Enquirer wrote that officers made no effort to save the prisoner "for a legal doom," and no report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage.

The first reports, a Chicago Tribune special dated July 8, a Courier-Journal special printed in Memphis on July 9 and an Atlanta wire carried in Sacramento, described a hanging. On July 9 the Savannah Morning News printed the LaGrange letter describing a burning, and from July 10 the Enquirer's longer burning account ran in Chicago, Ohio, Raleigh and Montana. The Tribune printed both versions unreconciled; burning excerpts ran into August.

Reprints headed the Enquirer account "Awful Vengeance"; it said the crime was so horrid that "the law's delays could not stand between him and vengeance." The Tribune called the hanging just retribution, the New Bloomfield Times headed its excerpt "A Merited Retribution," and the Clarksville Weekly Chronicle asked, "Who shall say his punishment was not just?" The Savannah Morning News called Waldrop "the demon," while the Alexandria Gazette noted that a report of oil being poured on him was "regarded as sensational."

The Courier-Journal special and the Tribune said Waldrop was hanged, while the LaGrange correspondent, the Enquirer and a July 11 Atlanta dispatch said he was burned; the burning accounts include the nearest, Georgia-based source. Locations also differ: most papers said Randolph County, Alabama, the Tribune Clay County, Alabama, a widely reprinted brief "Randolph County, Ga.," and the LaGrange letter and the Enquirer Heard County, Georgia. Dates range from Monday night, July 4, in most reports to the night of July 7 in the Enquirer and "the 8th inst." in a brief.

Savannah Morning News called him 'the demon' and 'a villain and murderer of the darkest character'.
